Textbook
A Rare and Hard-to-Hear Guidance
A Compass for the Direct Leap and Entry
Compiled and expounded by Zhanran

The content of this book is compiled from The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma and the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan. The author, Mr. Liu Zhuyuan (Master Changzong), is a sage of modern times, broadly versed in the scriptural canon and deeply learned in doctrine and contemplation; because he withdrew from the world and lived in seclusion, few knew of him. The depth of his practice and the loftiness of his realization may be seen in the following three points: First, the meaning and practice set forth in The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma and the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan. Master Yinguang praised him, saying: ‘Liu Zhuyuan’s literary and doctrinal understanding is very profound; seeing the recorded conduct of Mr. Zhang, I am filled with boundless admiration. Since the region of Sichuan has such a worthy, and he is also an advocate, it is truly the good fortune of the people of Sichuan, and likewise the good fortune of the Dharma.’ (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, First Letter in Reply to the Layman Xie Huilin) Second, ‘Therefore, in teaching people, he would always have them set everything down and contemplate their own mind. Those who followed this teaching, many attained awakening.’ (
The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma

) Third, ‘In the summer of 1950, the Master passed away at Baiyun Monastery; that night a white light shot up from the monastery toward the sky, and many saw it from near and afar.’ (Recorded in detail in Awakening to Sentiment, volume 11, issue 8)

In his later years the Master delighted in the joy of Chan and cared not for writing; only a few lecture manuscripts survived, which his disciples passed down by copying them from hand to hand; those who obtained them treasured them as something of inestimable worth. Fortunately, his disciple Mr. Jin Hongshu edited and published them, naming them The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma, and appended the eighteen letters in which the Master instructed him; only then did this black pearl come to light in the world.

The source text of this book is Mr. Liu Zhuyuan’s The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma. As the title indicates, this is the essential theory of the Buddha-Dharma and the essential practical cultivation. Though not lengthy in extent, it is vast and profound, advancing ever upward until it enters the stage of the Tathagata; it is the great and perfect Dharma.

blocks.text: A Brief Biography of the Master

inline.s: Mr. Liu Zhuyuan (

), styled Fuli, with the courtesy name Zhuyuan, and also known by the alias Liming, was a native of Zhongjiang County, Sichuan Province. In his youth he studied the Confucian classics and passed the examinations for the xiucai degree; because he excelled for years running in the annual examinations, he was recommended to the court (as a bagong scholar). Later he graduated from the College of Classics in Beijing, excelled in literature, and was thoroughly versed in the Three Rites. He served successively as a professor of literature at Sichuan Higher Normal College, Chengdu University, and Sichuan University, twenty years in all. In the twentieth year of the Republic of China (
) he resigned and entered the mountains to cultivate the Way.

[The bagong] In the Qing dynasty, the provincial education commissioners selected students who excelled in both letters and conduct and recommended them to the Imperial Academy (the highest seat of learning in the land) in the capital; these were called bagong students, abbreviated as bagong. [The Three Rites] is the collective name for the Confucian classics the Rites of Zhou, the Etiquette and Ceremonial, and the Record of Rites.

The Master’s study of Buddhism passed from Confucianism into Buddhism, and in Buddhist studies he was self-taught. In his letters he said: ‘In all my life I have had no master, though I first studied the classics. I used their method to read the books of the two schools of nature and characteristics, and to pursue the learning of the Tiantai and Xianshou schools. Later I entered the Chan school, whose gate is not elaborate, and so amid having no master, I found a master.’

[The two schools of nature and characteristics] are the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-characteristics school. [Tai and Xian] are the Tiantai school and the Xianshou school (that is, the Avatamsaka or Huayan school).
In the twenty-eighth year of the Guangxu reign (

), the Master was already propagating the Buddha-Dharma in Chengdu; the four assemblies looked up to him, and his affinity for the Dharma was exceedingly flourishing (see the Brief Chronological Table of Chinese Buddhism compiled by Tang Shengdi and others). After the founding of the Republic, while teaching at Chengdu University, he opened a lecture series on Buddhist studies on campus and publicly lectured on Buddhism, and was one of the first professors to bring Buddhist studies into the institutions of higher learning. He also established a Buddhist society in Chengdu and gathered assemblies to expound the scriptures and preach the Dharma. From the end of the Guangxu reign onward, over a span of more than twenty years, he exerted a considerable influence upon people in society; and those who, moved by him, took refuge in Buddhism were very many. The later famous master of Tibetan Buddhism, Neng Hai, while at Chengdu, heard the Master’s lecture and, inspired by it, shaved his head and left home.

In his early years the Master was expert in the Consciousness-Only (Vijnaptimatra) school, and once wrote An Outline of the Study of Consciousness-Only, of tens of thousands of words. He privately admired Yongming Yanshou, and in the twenty-first year of the Republic of China (

) wrote the Great Sectional Analysis of the Record of the Mirror of the Source. In his later years he delighted in the joy of Chan and cared not for authorship; only a few lecture manuscripts survived, copied and passed down by his disciples. In the thirty-seventh year (

), in the third lunar month, he shaved his head at Yanzuo Monastery in Xiaoquan, Deyang County, Sichuan, and received the triple-platform great precepts, his Dharma name being Changzong. Before long, at invitation, he lectured on the Surangama Sutra and transmitted the Pure Land contemplation method. Later he returned to Zhongjiang County, took up residence at Baiyun Monastery, and devoted himself to the study of the precepts. In the thirty-ninth year (

) he passed away, at the age of seventy-eight. Besides what has been recorded above, his works include the Detailed Sectional Analysis of the Record of the Mirror of the Source, about five fascicles, and the Method for Reading the Record of the Mirror of the Source, over ten fascicles. He also compiled the Dharma characteristics of the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom into the three volumes of the Dharma-Treasury of the Nature School, which, however, were never published.

[Privately admired (sishu)] means to revere and emulate someone privately without having formally become their disciple. [Yongming Yanshou] was the Chan master Yanshou of the Song dynasty, known as the Jue-wisdom (Zhijue) master; because he dwelt at Yongming Monastery on Mount Huiri in Hangzhou, he is called the Chan Master Yongming Yanshou. He was originally the third-generation master of the Fayan (Dharma-eye) school of the Chan tradition, but in Pure Land practice and Buddha-recitation he was also most diligent, making tens of thousands of recitations of the Buddha’s name his daily task; he composed the Four Boiled-Down Judgments, advocating the joint cultivation of Chan and the Pure Land, and he is the sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school. He has handed down the hundred-fascicle Record of the Mirror of the Source, the six-fascicle Collection of All Goodness Returning to the One, the one-fascicle Ode on the Spirit Dwelling in Peace and Bliss, the one-fascicle Verse on the Mind-Only, and others.

The sage Mr. Liu Zhuyuan, in his later years, left home and served as abbot of Baiyun Monastery (located in Zhongjiang County, Sichuan), taking the name Master Baiyun (White Cloud); hence his true transmission is called the ‘Essence of the White Cloud Mind.’ Its guiding principle is: directly contemplate your own mind, and seeing your nature, become a Buddha.

Why contemplate the mind? The Buddha-Dharma is vast, but its root is the mind; the gates of practice are measureless, but the principal one is contemplation. The ancients said: ‘If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no source.’ Because the Buddha-Dharma all rests upon the pure mind; only turning back to contemplate within and shine inward can one draw forth the Buddha-nature, and then all the gates of samadhi, all the gates of dharani, all the gates of liberation, and all the gates of supernormal power appear at once. Therefore know that the mind is the source of the wondrous Dharma: if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn forth? Hence contemplation of the mind is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddha-Dharma, which no other practice can match.
To contemplate and reflect constantly is for prajna to perfume ignorance.

Once ignorance is broken, the Dharma-body manifests at once (clear the mind and see one’s nature). Directly leaping into the stage of the Tathagata, without passing through the asamkhya kalpas, one attains the Dharma-body.

[Contemplating the mind] means to observe one’s own mind. The mind is the lord of all dharmas, and no thing is ever outside the mind; therefore, to contemplate the mind is to contemplate everything. The Sutra of the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle says:
‘Among the three realms, the mind is the sovereign; one who can contemplate the mind gains ultimate liberation, and one who cannot forever remains in bondage.’
Again it says:
‘Beholding the marks, one arouses the mind and removes wrong views; one should dwell in the forest retreat and contemplate one’s own mind.’
[Lanruo] is aranya, rendered in Chinese as ‘a place of stillness.’
[Sengqi] is an abbreviation of ‘asamkhya kalpas.’

Moreover, to arouse the bodhi mind is to contemplate the mind of pure self-nature (see in detail the chapter ‘Arousing the Bodhi Mind’). The merit of arousing the bodhi mind is supremely excellent beyond compare; it cannot be described fully, for it pervades all the scriptures and is set forth widely in the Avatamsaka, the Yogacara, the Prajnaparamita, and the other treatises. For example: ‘One who arouses the bodhi mind is prophesied by all the Buddhas and receives the protection of all the Buddhas.’ At the first arousal of the mind, the Buddha gives the prophecy; this is clearly stated in all the scriptures, such as the Sutra of the Arousing of the Bodhi Mind, the Sutra of the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle, and the Sutra of Questions on the Meaning of the Wise; it is most fully set forth in the Avatamsaka Sutra. As for the protection of all the Buddhas, the Lankavatara Sutra says: ‘In all the lands of the ten directions, all the measureless Buddhas extend their hands of light and touch the crown of this person’s head.’ Thus all the Buddhas constantly protect such a practitioner. (See the section ‘The Merit of Arousing the Mind’.)

The characteristic of the ‘White Cloud Mind-Essentials’ is sharp, swift, sudden, and perfect. How great is the fortune of one who reads and practices it! One should advance in both understanding and practice together: to understand is to put into practice, and to practice is to understand. Doing the work of tuning and taming each day, with thoughts clarified, wisdom arises; not departing from self-nature, one is a field of merit. When one contemplates to the point that a single thought does not arise, one accords with prajna. The Mahavairocana Sutra says: ‘What is bodhi? It is knowing one’s own mind as it really is.’ The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: ‘All Tathagatas, in the causal ground from which they originate, all rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-Way.’

The Essentials of the Mind Transmission says: ‘Apart from all marks, sentient beings and Buddhas are no different; one who can be without mind is at the ultimate. If a student of the Way does not directly become without mind, though he cultivate through many kalpas he will never accomplish the Way, for he is bound by the works of the three vehicles and cannot gain liberation. Yet there are those who realize this mind quickly or slowly: some, upon hearing the Dharma, become without mind in a single thought; some reach the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications before becoming without mind; some reach the ten grounds before becoming without mind. Whether it takes long or short, it is only upon becoming without mind that one settles; there is nothing further to cultivate or realize. In truth there is nothing attained, and this is real and not false. To attain it in a single thought and to attain it upon the ten grounds are exactly equal in function, with no gradation of shallow or deep — it is merely that through the kalpas one has vainly undergone hardship.’

View, practice, and fruit are the three essential elements of the bodhi path. ‘View’ is understanding. First, understanding must be correct. How to realize the ‘view’ — this is ‘practice.’ Having realized the ‘view’ — this is ‘fruit.’ The White Cloud Dharma-gate is to be understood thus, and practiced thus.
Question: Will contemplating the mind cause one to stagnate on the path of practice?

The Editor answers: The essential point of the method of contemplating the mind is, toward thoughts, to ‘know them but not follow them.’ And the most crucial thing is the ‘knowing’ — to keep constantly aware of thoughts; as long as one maintains awareness of thoughts, one will naturally not follow them. Moreover, the power of awareness is constantly increasing; once it has grown strong to a certain degree, one can realize a thought the instant it arises and, realizing it, have it vanish at once. When the practice has fused into a single whole, one turns the light back and shines it inward: ‘Who, in the end, is this one who is aware?’ Practicing thus for a long time, when the melon is ripe the stem falls of itself, and one directly sees the original face. Therefore, grasping the essential point of contemplating the mind, one will not stagnate on the path. If one forgets the awareness, then unless one is in a state of scattering, one falls into dullness and torpor.
Question: Is there any contradiction between contemplating the mind and holding the name and reciting the Buddha?
Answer: Not only is there no contradiction, but the two aid each other. The Essential Anthology of the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, in the section on the
Showing the Method of Practice, says:

‘When one first begins to recite the Buddha, before having personally realized samadhi, who can be free of deluded thoughts? What is valuable is that the mind is constantly aware and illumining, not turning to follow delusions.’

This ‘mind constantly aware and illumining, not turning to follow delusions’ is precisely the contemplation of the mind. With the skill of contemplating the mind, to recite the Buddha is like a tiger that has grown horns; try it yourself and you will know. Moreover, to recite the Buddha and understand the first meaning, and attain the upper-grade rebirth — this is clearly recorded in the Contemplation Sutra.

Question: Then why did Master Yinguang say: ‘Do not use the method of contemplating the mind in recitation; you should use the method of gathering the mind in recitation.’ (From the Letter in Reply to the Layman Yang Weizhang)

Answer: Because the other party (the layman Yang Weizhang) was a beginner in the study, without sufficient foundation, yet used the method of contemplating the mind to recite the Buddha, which caused the fire of the heart to blaze upward. So in this letter, Master Yinguang was addressing the other party’s specific situation, prescribing medicine according to the illness, and not negating the method of contemplating the mind to recite the Buddha. Master Yinguang wrote: “
You, an ordinary being of extremely heavy karmic power,
vainly use
the method of contemplating the mind,
and so have brought this upon yourself
(that is, the ‘fire of the heart blazing upward’ mentioned in the other party’s letter)
.” And he continued to write: “The method of contemplating the mind is the method of contemplation used by the doctrinal schools; for a person who recites the Buddha,
it is not quite suited to their capacity

.” Here, ‘for a person who recites the Buddha, it is not quite suited to their capacity’ is a tactful way of saying that your faculties do not measure up to contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha, and so the fire of the heart blazed upward. Therefore
Master Yinguang told him:
“Do not use the method of contemplating the mind in recitation; you should use the method of gathering the mind in recitation.”

Contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha is most wondrous, yet it is not suited to those without sufficient foundation. Because beginner students lack a sufficient foundation, if they contemplate the mind while reciting the Buddha, they will often experience dizziness, headaches, the fire of the heart blazing upward, and such symptoms. Therefore, the book Aware Recitation of the Buddha, when it speaks of ‘being aware of the present thought (contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha),’ has already laid a solid foundation through the preliminary chapter of training (being aware of movement, being aware of sensation, being aware of breathing, being aware of the present moment, being aware of the mind-thoughts) and through ‘being aware of the Buddha-name.’ In the Record of Groping for the Image of the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, Master Yinguang instructs:
“As for the method,
one must

at the time of reciting, with each recitation turn back and contemplate, concentrating on a single realm, not allowing the mind to race outward, thought after thought watching over the source of the mind, mind after mind in accord with the Buddha-body.”
Is this not contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha? Therefore, for a person who recites the Buddha to adopt the method of contemplating the mind, one must first have a certain foundation.

Contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha is the very essence of holding the name and reciting the Buddha. Since ancient times, many ancestral masters and great worthies have attained single-minded and undisturbed concentration through contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha.
As for the supreme importance of contemplating the mind, Master Yinguang, describing how Sakyamuni Buddha attained the Way, wrote: ‘At the age of nine-

teen, at midnight on the eighth day of the second month, he rode the horse Kanthaka, leapt over the city walls and departed, went straight into the deep mountains, and cultivated the transcendent Way. Again, wishing to show that those of the externalist paths were all not the right Dharma, he wandered for another five years, visiting all the ascetic sages. Later he
sat alone contemplating the mind,
eating but one

sesame and one grain of wheat a day, practicing austerities for six years; and at dawn on the eighth day of the twelfth month, when the morning star arose, he looked up and was suddenly, greatly enlightened. He exclaimed: ‘How wondrous, how wondrous! All sentient beings are endowed with the wisdom and virtue-marks of the Tathagata. Only because of deluded thoughts and clinging can they not realize it. If they were free of deluded thoughts, then all-knowledge, natural knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge would appear at once.’
(A Lecture at the Chaoyang Buddhist Society
No. 1)
Question: What is the relationship between contemplating the mind and practicing the Pure Land?

Answer: For the one who contemplates the mind, the mind is the Pure Land; to contemplate it is precisely faith, vow, and practice, and one is reborn in the Pure Land. The mind is the Tathagata-nature, the Buddha-nature, which is itself the land; therefore, arousing the bodhi mind is the supreme and true Buddha-recitation Dharma-gate. To arouse the bodhi mind is to be mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha. To be mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha is to recite the Buddha by means of reality, the so-called one-vehicle Buddha-recitation, which is the most supreme of the Pure Land school.

[Arousing the bodhi mind] The full name is to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, abbreviated as arousing the mind. The bodhi mind is the mind of pure self-nature. This mind of pure self-nature is equal in sentient beings and Buddhas, possessed by all, neither increasing nor decreasing. ‘Arouse’ means to initiate, to develop. To arouse the bodhi mind is to initiate and develop the mind of pure self-nature. The first stirring is merely the initiating; seeing one’s nature is called the developing. Yet without contemplation one cannot initiate it, and without contemplation one cannot develop it. Therefore, to arouse the bodhi mind is to contemplate this mind of pure self-nature. The Mahavairocana Sutra says: ‘What is bodhi? It is knowing one’s own mind as it really is.’ [Reciting the Buddha by means of reality]
This is to recite the Buddha by means of the dharmas that are ultimately empty and without any existence.

In the Buddha-Treasury Sutra, the Buddha says: ‘Sariputra, what is called being mindful of the Buddha? To see that there is nothing that exists — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, the Buddhas are measureless, inconceivable, incalculable; for this reason, to see that nothing exists is called being mindful of the Buddha. The reality is without discrimination; the Buddhas are without discrimination. Therefore it is said: to be mindful without discrimination is to be mindful of the Buddha. Again, to see the reality of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, and nothing exists.
Thus by the dharmas that are ultimately empty and that do not exist, one is mindful of the Buddha.

Again, in such dharmas, even a small thought cannot be obtained — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, this Dharma of mindfulness of the Buddha cuts off the path of speech, transcends all thoughts, and cannot be grasped by thought — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, all thoughts have the mark of still extinction. To accord with this Dharma is called practicing the mindfulness of the Buddha. One cannot be mindful of the Buddha by form; why? To be mindful of form is to grasp at a mark, and to relish the flavor is to be consciousness. Having no form, no color, no condition, no nature — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Therefore know: without discrimination, without grasping, without rejecting — this is truly being mindful of the Buddha.’ ‘Mindfulness of the Buddha is called the destruction of all the considerations of good and evil; without considerations, without reflection, still and without thought — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Why? One should not recall the Buddhas by considerations and reflections; without considerations and without reflection is called pure mindfulness of the Buddha. In this mindfulness there is not even the subtle mind, thought, and karmic activity — how much the less the actions of body and speech!’ ‘All these dharmas are empty, having no real nature; one cannot be mindful of a single mark, that which is spoken of as markless — this is called true mindfulness of the Buddha. That is, no birth, no extinction, no mark, no effort.’ [Considerations and reflections (jueguan)] In the newer translations this is ‘vitarka-vicara’ (initial and sustained application), and in the older translations it is ‘jueguan.’ Coarse thought is called ‘jue’ (initial) and fine thought is called ‘guan’ (sustained); both can disturb the concentrated mind. [Being mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha is precisely reciting the Buddha by means of reality, the so-called one-vehicle Buddha-recitation, which is the most supreme of the Pure Land school] Master Lianchi, in his Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra, says: ‘Know that the Pure Land is mind-only; there is no external realm beyond it.’ ‘In accord with principle, self-nature returns to the original body — this is the meaning of vowing to be born in that land.’

blocks.text: Chapter One. The Outline of Studying Buddhism

inline.s: The outline of studying Buddhism: First, for what purpose? To clarify the mind and see the nature. Second, on what principle? On the principle of the two emptinesses. Third, what practice? To cultivate the practice of prajna. Fourth, to what dharma to awaken? To awaken to the dharmas that arise through conditions.

blocks.text: 1. For What Purpose: To Clarify the Mind and See the Nature

inline.s: In recent times people’s minds are much given to the Buddha-Dharma: some keep a family shrine to the Buddha, some make pilgrimages to the mountains and burn incense, some diligently practice giving, some cultivate offerings, some receive the three refuges, some observe the five precepts, some recite the scriptures and the Buddha-name, some hold mantras and practice the Dharma, some deeply study the doctrinal principles, and some exclusively practice Chan contemplation. Though their ways differ in many respects, in believing the Buddha they are one.

I now wish to ask a question: You, gentlemen, practice thus diligently — for what purpose, in the end? You weary your bodies and exhaust your spirits, spending your energy and days without complaint; what is your aim? They will say: ‘We have heard that the Buddha-Dharma is extraordinary, and so we like it; it has become the fashion in the world, and we follow the crowd.’ I say: This is not an answer to my question.

Again they say: ‘We wish to escape suffering.’ The poor wish to gain wealth; the sick wish to pray for recovery; those in distress hope for success; the fallen long for deliverance. I say: These words are close, but still not the true answer.

Again they say: ‘We wish to remove karmic hindrances. The suffering of this life is all brought about by the evil karma of former lives. Now we will abandon evil and cultivate good, hoping that the karmic hindrances may be removed and we avoid the retribution of suffering.’ I say: These words seem right, but they are still not complete.

Again they say: ‘We wish to cut off afflictions. Human beings create karma because of afflictions. Now we will extinguish the afflictions, so that the bitter fruit no longer arises.’ I say: These words seem right, but they are still not complete.

They startle and say: ‘To cut off afflictions, to remove karmic hindrances, to leave suffering and attain bliss — this is the orthodox aim of the Buddha-Dharma; how is it still not complete? Giving, observing precepts, worship and offerings, reciting the scriptures and the Buddha-name, holding mantras and practicing contemplation — these are the orthodox practices of the Buddha-Dharma; how are they still not complete? With these we will save ourselves and save others; how could there still be any regret?’

I say: Be a little calm and do not be impatient; I will speak it for you. Generally, in discussing principles one must trace them to their root; in doing things one must ask their reason. What you have spoken of does have meaning within the Buddha-Dharma, but it is the branches and leaves, the minor details. If one practices in this direction, though one’s resolve be good, one wastes one’s energy. The scripture says: ‘Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called giving. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called offering.’ I now take this as an example and add a few more words: Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called observing the precepts. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called worship. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called reciting the scriptures. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called being mindful of the Buddha. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called holding mantras. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called practicing contemplation. You have not spoken of the real place, and so I do not approve. The scripture says: ‘If the causal ground is not true, the fruit is twisted and crooked.’ Again it says: ‘If one wishes to cultivate the great practice, one must know the dharma-practice of the causal ground.’ People of the world, dull and confused, do not seek this, and so they labor in vain to no benefit. Now for you all I will make clear the real, and you will gain twice the result with half the effort.

The real Dharma is our own mind. Because this mind has the nature of awareness, it is called the Buddha-nature. Because it is the root of all dharmas, it is called the Dharma-body. Because it never changes, it is called true thusness. Because its nature is not false, it is called reality. Because it knows everything, it is called bodhi. (Bodhi is right wisdom, and therefore it knows everything.) Because it is still and unmoving, it is called nirvana. The nature of all dharmas is called the Dharma-nature. All these various names are but different names for our true mind. All people originally possess it, and each is perfectly complete in it; it is close within the mind, needing no distant search. To become a Buddha or a patriarch is this one mind, which the Chan school calls ‘clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.’ The mind is the nature (mind and nature are one; this comes from the Avatamsaka Sutra)

; the so-called real Dharma is this mind. We all have this mind, yet do not know it ourselves, and suffer through long kalpas — is this not pitiable? Studying Buddhism is nothing other than clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. If one clarifies the mind and sees the nature, then afflictions are cut off by themselves without waiting to be cut, karmic hindrances are removed by themselves without waiting to be removed, all sufferings are extinguished by themselves without waiting to be extinguished, the three jewels are offered to without need of speaking of offering — one has already offered to the three jewels of one’s own mind; one gives without giving a single coin and yet the giving surpasses the seven jewels; one holds no mantra and yet spontaneously attains the seal and the mantric power; one recites no scripture and yet the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all penetrated. If one sets to work from the root, the fruit is great and the merit lofty thus; you gentlemen, how can you not take it up?

The ancients said: Sentient beings exist through karma; karma exists through delusion; delusion exists through consciousness; consciousness exists through the mind; and the mind is the final, ultimate place. If one does not penetrate this one key point, the consciousness persists, afflictions are cut off only to arise again, karmic hindrances are dispelled only to spring up again, and the bitter fruit is never removed. It is like felling a tree: if you cut off only its branches and leaves, it grows again the next year — when will there be an end? If you cut off its root and stalk, it will never sprout again. Therefore, when the Buddha said that without knowing the real Dharma it is not called giving or offering, the intent was to spur the people of the world to know that the real place lies in our own mind. (This meaning comes from the Avatamsaka Sutra and the Prajnaparamita sutras; the passages are very extensive and one may study them.) Otherwise, one cultivates the cause without the fruit. Why? Because the fruit lies in the real place. (Note: one must apply effort in the real place before the fruit can come about.) Otherwise (note: if not so), the scripture says the mind is the source of evil and the body is the gathering place of offenses. (Note: this mind is the consciousness-mind, distinct from the true mind above.) If one has not understood where the real place is, how can one cut off afflictions, remove karmic hindrances, and escape the sea of suffering? As for what purpose one studies — it is to seek to clarify the mind and see the nature.

blocks.text: 2. On What Principle: On the Principle of the Two Emptinesses

title: The Essence of the White Cloud Mind (A Precious Manual of Mind-Contemplation)
author: Dankan Zixin (Just Contemplate Your Own Mind)
excerpt: The content of this book is compiled from The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma and the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan. The author, Mr. Liu Zhuyuan (Master Changzong), is a sage of modern times, broadly versed in the scriptural canon, deeply learned in doctrine and contemplation; because he withdrew from the world and lived in seclusion, few knew of him. The depth of his practice and the loftiness of his realization may be seen in the following three points: First, the Buddha-
